messages.content: Can you retrieve the weather forecast for White Plains for next week with temperatures in Celsius?

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.reasoning:
We need to call the function requests_get with appropriate parameters. The user wants forecast for White Plains next week with temperatures in Celsius. We need to find latitude and longitude for White Plains. White Plains is a city in New York, USA. Approx coordinates: 41.0536° N, 73.7629° W. So latitude 41.0536, longitude -73.7629. Use Open-Meteo API. The endpoint likely is "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast". We need to set params: latitude, longitude, daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min, maybe also temperature_2m_mean? But we want forecast for next week. We can set start_date and end_date. For next week, we need dates. Let's assume today is 2026-10-09. Next week would be 2026-10-10 to 2026-10-16 inclusive. So start_date=2026-10-10, end_date=2026-10-16. Also set timezone=America/New_York. And units=metric. Actually Open-Meteo uses "daily" param for variables. For temperature, we can use "temperature_2m_max" and "temperature_2m_min". Also "temperature_2m_mean" maybe not available. We'll just provide max and min. Also "temperature_2m_max" and "temperature_2m_min" are part of daily. So daily="temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min". Also "temperature_2m_max" returns max temp in Celsius if units=metric. So we set "daily_units" maybe not needed. The API supports "temperature_unit=metric". Actually the parameter is "temperature_unit=metric" or "temperature_unit=imperial"? Let's check. According to Open-Meteo docs, you can set "temperature_unit=metric" to get Celsius. So we add that param. Also "timezone=America/New_York". So final params: latitude=41.0536, longitude=-73.7629, daily="temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min", start_date="2026-10-10", end_date="2026-10-16", temperature_unit="metric", timezone="America/New_York". Also maybe "precipitation_probability" but not needed.

Thus we call function.
